Before the first dawn, the world was a silent bowl of stone. No river moved, no bird called, and the sky hung low, dark and empty. In a cave beneath the tallest mountain lived Luma, a small fox with silver paws. Though all creatures slept in the deep quiet, Luma stayed awake, listening for a sound that had not yet been born.

One night she found a coal glowing in the mountain’s heart. It pulsed like a tiny sun. Luma carried it carefully in her mouth and climbed to the peak. The coal burned her tongue, but she did not let it fall. At the summit, she leapt upward and struck the low sky with her silver paws.

The coal shattered into a thousand sparks. Some became stars. One became the moon. The brightest rolled to the eastern edge of the world and grew into the sun.

Light spilled over the stones, and the stones wept their first tears, which became rivers. Birds woke and sang. Trees lifted their arms.

Since then, foxes run at twilight, when sun and stars share the sky, remembering Luma, who gave the world its first morning.

Before the first dawn, the world was a silent bowl of stone, and all creatures moved by touch. In the deepest cave lived Luma, a small moth with wings as pale as ash. Though she could not see, she dreamed of colors that had no names.

One night, Luma heard the mountains weeping. “We are tired of holding up the dark,” they groaned. So she flew upward, higher than any bird, guided only by the sorrow in their voices. At the roof of the sky she found a sleeping ember curled inside a shell of ice.

Luma beat her fragile wings against the ice for seven days. On the eighth, the shell cracked, and the ember opened its golden eye. Heat poured out, becoming the first sun. Its light struck Luma’s wings, scattering into red, blue, green, and violet. The colors fell to earth and painted rivers, leaves, feathers, and flowers.

But Luma had flown too close. Her wings turned to silver dust, and she drifted down as moonlight. That is why moths still chase lamps: they are searching for Luma, their brave ancestor, who taught the dark to shine and gave the world its colors forever.

Mountains crouched like sleeping giants, rivers forgot how to run, and every creature knew only the shape of darkness. Luma fell as glittering dust, becoming the moon’s soft glow. So moths still circle every candle, believing one small flame may hide another dawn, and that bravery can hatch light from ice.
